analysis.one_liner: Requires regulators to weigh labor standards before granting foreign airlines access to U.S. routes.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee that received it; it got no hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When the Transportation Department decides whether to let a foreign airline fly in U.S. air space, the bill would require it to consider whether that airline's operations undermine labor standards. It would also add protecting labor standards to the official goals the State Department and DOT follow when negotiating U.S. international aviation agreements, alongside the existing goals of promoting competition. The aim is to stop foreign carriers from gaining access to U.S. markets by basing crews in low-wage countries with weak labor rules, which undercuts U.S. airline workers.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. airline employees — pilots, flight attendants, and ground workers — gain a legal safeguard against foreign competitors using flag-of-convenience arrangements to keep wages down and take flying jobs away from workers paid under U.S. and international labor standards. U.S. airlines that pay for their labor also gain a more level competitive field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds 'preventing the undermining of labor standards' as a factor the DOT must consider in the public-interest test for foreign air carrier permits [S2][S3].

It also adds the same labor-standards factor to the statutory principles the State Department and DOT must follow when formulating U.S. international air transportation policy and negotiating aviation agreements [S2][S3].

Together, these changes give U.S. officials explicit legal authority to deny or condition market access for foreign carriers whose business model depends on weak labor rules, a tool current law does not clearly provide [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign air carriers whose business models rely on basing crews in low-wage countries would face stricter review or denial of access to the U.S. market. Travelers could face somewhat higher fares to the extent those carriers had been lowering prices through lower labor costs.

drawbacks.text: Adding labor standards to the public-interest test could limit airline competition, and restricting foreign carriers' access could mean higher fares and fewer choices for U.S. travelers — a cost an honest supporter must weigh against protecting jobs and wages.

The bill gives regulators broad discretion without defining 'labor standards,' leaving outcomes dependent on how each administration applies the factor — supporters of the current more purely pro-competition policy would argue that uncertainty itself deters investment and cooperation with trading partners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers whose jobs and pay are at stake, the safeguard is direct and the bill is narrowly written: it does not block foreign carriers, it only adds labor standards to an existing review. The real cost falls on travelers only to the degree that foreign carriers' lower-cost service was sustained by weak labor rules. The bill's main weakness is not design but neglect — it sat without a hearing, so its merits were never tested in a hearing record or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill twice and sent it to the Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or moved it before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Klobuchar introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, with Republican Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas as the other original sponsor [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S5].
That referral was the last action ever taken: the bill received no markup, no hearing record, and no floor vote in the Senate or House before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
The committee that received the bill has jurisdiction over aviation policy and never scheduled it for consideration during the two-year Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign air carriers using low-wage, weak-labor crew arrangements keep unrestricted access to the U.S. market, and no regulator gains a labor-standards tool; U.S. airline workers get no new protection. Supporters would note the same result follows from the committee's inaction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign carriers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — and the bill was never opposed on any recorded vote; it simply died in committee without a hearing.

industries.industry: Foreign air carriers operating in the U.S. market
industries.note: The bill would let DOT deny or condition permits for carriers whose labor practices undercut standards, targeting business models built on crewing flights in low-wage countries. Their gain from the status quo comes at the cost of U.S. airline jobs and pay.

U.S. airlines that pay market-rate wages would face less competition from carriers holding labor costs down through flag-of-convenience structures. Their competitive interest runs alongside the wage interests of their employees, though travelers could see fewer low-cost options.

The bill adds labor standards as an explicit factor in foreign carrier permits and trade negotiations, giving workers' representatives a legal hook to challenge arrangements that outsource their jobs. This is the constituency the bill was written for.
